reason: The cited evidence (E1) shows thermal-aging-induced phase segregation and softening in a refractory HEA at 700°C, but it does not involve mechanical loading or demonstrate stress-assisted segregation, brittle precipitate formation, or toughness reduction. E2 describes phase separation in an as-cast HEA wire and deformation-induced twinning, but it does not address stress-induced segregation from an initially single-phase state or brittle fracture. Thus, the key premises linking mechanical stress to segregation, brittle phase nucleation, and toughness loss are unsupported by the cited passages.
premises: Stress-assisted compositional segregation can occur in single-phase HEAs under demanding mechanical service
This segregation leads to nucleation of nanoscale brittle second-phase precipitates
These precipitates act as crack initiation sites and reduce toughness
The mechanism is driven by local stress concentrations accelerating diffusion or activating plasticity
The phenomenon occurs at moderately elevated temperatures (300–700°C) under high loads
